section_summary: This section contains U.S. Embassy Tokyo monthly reports and State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda from November 1934 to February 1935 covering Japanese political, diplomatic, and economic developments. Key international matters include Japan's formal abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty, negotiations and protests concerning the Japanese Petroleum Industry Law and the Manchukuo Oil Monopoly, the completed sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway by Soviet Russia to Manchukuo, and armed border incidents in Jehol and Lake Buir. Domestically, the reports trace the passage of the national budget and relief appropriations, Korekiyo Takahashi's fiscal stewardship and warnings against capital outflow, the rivalry between the Seiyukai and Minseito parties, and government efforts to regulate violent Rightist societies.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of the monthly report on political, financial, and economic conditions in Japan for November 1934.
subfiles.from: Embassy of the United States of America, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Covers the Cabinet's approval of an emergency tax on profits and the 1935-36 national budget, as well as the resignation of Finance Minister Sadanobu Fujii and his replacement by Korekiyo Takahashi. Reviews favorable trade statistics, the application of the Major Industry Control Law to cement manufacturing, and a motorcade blunder during the Emperor's visit to Gumma Prefecture that prompted official apologies and an attempted suicide. Concludes with complete schedules of telegrams (Nos. 243-265) and despatches (Nos. 1030-1074) sent to the State Department during November 1934.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of November, 1934 (Report No. 98)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum highlighting significant points in the Tokyo Embassy's December 1934 monthly report.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for December 1934 was substantially condensed to approximately one-third its former length to conform with Department guidelines. Draws particular attention to Japanese Foreign Office statements on provocative rhetoric across the Pacific, the cancellation of a British antimony concession in Hunan following Japanese consular protests, thirty-year land leases granted to Japanese in North Manchuria, and the failure to open the Kobe shipping conference with the Netherlands over language disagreements. Also notes the War Office's drafting of Japan's first national air defense legislation.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for December, 1934

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting Report No. 99 reviewing Japanese foreign relations, domestic politics, and economic conditions during December 1934.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1136 transmits Report No. 99, detailing Japan's formal denunciation of the Washington Naval Treaty following unanimous Privy Council approval, public reaction to Representative Vinson's statements on a Nicaraguan canal, and joint diplomatic representations over the Petroleum Industry Law and Manchukuo Oil Monopoly. Examines ongoing negotiations for the transfer of the Chinese Eastern Railway, the appointment of General Jiro Minami as Kwantung Army Commander and Ambassador to Manchukuo, the conviction of the Kaiun Maru crew in Formosa, and the exposure of a Rightist assassination plot against Prince Saionji, Count Makino, and other leaders. Includes complete lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 1075-1119) and telegrams (Nos. 266-287) transmitted during December.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1136 Transmitting Report No. 99 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of December, 1934
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum evaluating key foreign policy and domestic political items in Tokyo's January 1935 monthly report.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes Japanese policy regarding League of Nations assistance to China, the collapse of Japanese-Dutch shipping negotiations over language selection, and growing Japanese diplomatic, military, and educational influence in Siam. Evaluates the Cabinet's plan to create an advisory National Policy Commission, drawing comparisons to the 1917 Diplomatic Advisory Body dismantled by Takashi Hara as evidence of the weakened standing of political parties. Notes the resignation of Baron Wakatsuki and assumption of the Minseito presidency by Chuji Machida, as well as economic indicators pointing to decelerating growth.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for January, 1935

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch forwarding Report No. 100 detailing Japanese external relations, legislative developments, and economic affairs during January 1935.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Presents Report No. 100, which reviews Japanese interpretations of statements by Norman Davis regarding naval ratios, conversations on the Petroleum Industry Law, and prison sentences handed down in Formosa to the crew of the Kaiun Maru. Details Kwantung Army operations expelling General Sung Che-yuan's troops from western Jehol, rumors of a comprehensive Sino-Japanese rapprochement, Soviet-Manchukuo agreement on terms for purchasing the Chinese Eastern Railway, and a border engagement near Lake Buir. In domestic affairs, discusses the 67th Diet session, Takahashi's defense of government financial policy alongside cautions against over-investing in Manchukuo, Chuji Machida assuming the Minseito presidency, proposed legislation curbing violent Rightist groups, and appends monthly lists of despatches (Nos. 1120-1151) and telegrams (Nos. 1-21).
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1161 Transmitting Report No. 100 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of January, 1935
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing principal developments in Tokyo's monthly report for February 1935.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the February 1935 monthly report, noting Ambassador Grew's representations regarding three Americans mistreated by Osaka police and the subsequent dismissal of assault charges against them. Analyzes Japanese press speculation concerning a Sino-Japanese rapprochement, observing that the Foreign Office and Navy are optimistic about Chinese overtures while the Army remains skeptical. Highlights statements by the Navy Minister regarding a potential Pacific defense pact covering Hawaii and Singapore, police and Home Office opposition to the Justice Ministry's bill against Rightist organizations, and proposed budget appropriations to expand commercial air routes over fifteen years.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for February, 1935

subfiles.about: Cover despatch and title page transmitting the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan for February 1935.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1205 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits to Secretary of State Cordell Hull the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report (Report No. 101) on political, economic, and general conditions in Japan for the month of February 1935. The transmittal specifies distribution copies to diplomatic and consular posts in Peiping, Moscow, Shanghai, Mukden, Harbin, Kobe, and Dairen, and is accompanied by the formal cover title page of Report No. 101.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1205 Transmitting Report No. 101 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of February, 1935
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington
